title: The analysis and utilization of cycling training data
authors: Jobson SA, Passfield L, Atkinson G, Barton G, Scarf P
population: Not applicable (review of training-dose quantification methods and mathematical training-performance models, focused on cycling)
findings: Volume (km or h per week) is an index of training dose used with some success but usually fails to accommodate training intensity; session RPE and heart-rate TRIMP are alternatives that capture intensity.
An exponentially weighted averaging process can represent variable power output as 'normalized power'.

Impulse-response models take into account the dynamic and temporal characteristics of training, but have significant limitations such as an excessive number of performance tests needed to determine model parameters.

Non-linear artificial neural networks may describe the adaptation process more accurately but are constrained by the large number of datasets needed to train them; PerPot, mixed linear modelling, cluster analysis and chaos theory need much further research before they can be considered alternatives.
limitations: 2009 narrative review, cycling-centred; predates modern wearables and regularised ML work.
implications: Quantify load with an intensity-aware metric (HR TRIMP or session RPE) rather than volume alone.
Expect high data demands from both impulse-response and neural-network approaches; plan fallbacks for athletes with sparse performance tests.
